question: Move the AED at M.S. 224 Manhattan East School for Arts & Academics into a 24/7 outdoor cabinet on the building's street wall.

evidence.text: M.S. 224 Manhattan East School for Arts & Academics (School, ZIP 10029) has a registered AED at "Main Entrance by School Safety; Outside Room 263; 3rd Fl Outside RM 310; 4th Floor Outside 456; 5th fl Outside RM 510".
Its hours come from: School building assumed open 7 AM to 6 PM on school days, September to June. Move the school-hours control to test other closing times.
Under that assumption it is reachable 55 of 168 hours in a school-year week, and 0 hours in a summer week if it is a school.
In 2025, an expected 1.48 cardiac-arrest 911 calls a year came from inside its two-minute walking area at hours when every AED in reach was shut (rank 2 of 100 NYC schools).
Within 400 m there are 6 other registered AED locations; 0 of them are open 24/7 by their published hours.
Citywide, a time-blind map puts 4.6% of call-weighted area within a two-minute walk of an AED; at the hour calls actually came in, 1.4% was within reach of one confirmed open.
Published research: a bystander shock with a public AED was associated with survival to discharge of 66.5% versus 43.0% without (Pollack et al., Circulation 2018, observed shockable public arrests).
Overture Maps lists FDNY EMS Station 10, a fire station normally staffed around the clock, 136 m away: a possible alternative host for a 24/7 AED.
Unknown to this data: cabinet cost, vandalism risk, whether the school already allows after-hours access, and the actual location of each 2025 call inside the ZIP (only ZIP-level data is public).

turns.speaker: advocate
turns.text: Moving this AED to a 24/7 outdoor cabinet directly addresses a documented gap in emergency response. The school's current indoor placement is reachable only 55 of 168 hours weekly during the school year, and zero hours in summer [E2, E3]. This matters because the area experienced an expected 1.48 cardiac-arrest calls annually during hours when every nearby AED was closed [E4]—ranking second among 100 NYC schools for this problem. Research shows bystander shock with a public AED reaches 66.5% survival versus 43.0% without [E7]. While FDNY Station 10 sits nearby [E8], a street-wall cabinet ensures immediate access regardless of station staffing. The six other AEDs in range are all closed after hours [E5], leaving residents vulnerable when citywide only 1.4% of actual call locations reach an open AED [E6].

turns.speaker: skeptic
turns.text: The case for moving this AED rests on incomplete data and unexamined costs. Yes, the school's current placement reaches only 55 of 168 weekly hours [E2, E3], but we don't know where last year's 1.48 calls actually occurred within the ZIP—only that they happened somewhere in the area [E9]. FDNY Station 10 sits just 136 meters away and is staffed around the clock [E8], potentially offering a faster, lower-cost alternative than installing and maintaining a street cabinet. We also lack critical information: cabinet installation and vandalism costs, whether after-hours school access is already feasible, and whether the school would even permit outdoor installation [E9]. Before committing resources here, we should explore whether the fire station can host an AED and compare total costs against the documented but geographically uncertain need.

turns.speaker: advocate
turns.text: The skeptic's point about FDNY Station 10 deserves serious consideration, but it doesn't eliminate the case for a street cabinet. Station 10 is 136 meters away [E8], which exceeds the two-minute walking radius where this AED would be most effective during cardiac arrest—time is critical, and even a nearby station requires someone to retrieve the device and return. The school's current placement reaches zero hours in summer [E3], yet cardiac arrests don't stop then. A street-wall cabinet at M.S. 224 ensures immediate public access year-round, whereas relying on the fire station requires coordination and travel time we can't guarantee. The area ranked second among 100 NYC schools for calls during hours when all nearby AEDs were closed [E4]. Yes, we lack cabinet costs and exact call locations [E9], but those are implementation details—they don't negate the documented gap. The skeptic is right that we should explore the fire station option in parallel, but a 24/7 outdoor cabinet directly solves the access problem the data shows.

turns.speaker: skeptic
turns.text: The advocate makes a fair point that 136 meters exceeds the ideal two-minute radius and that fire station retrieval takes time we can't control. But that's precisely why we need the missing data before deciding [E9]. We don't know the actual cost of a street cabinet, its vandalism risk in this neighborhood, or whether the school would even permit it—those aren't minor details, they're the foundation of a sound decision. More importantly, we don't know where last year's 1.48 calls actually occurred within the ZIP [E9]. If most happened near the fire station rather than near the school, moving the AED solves nothing. The advocate is right that summer cardiac arrests don't stop, but the fire station is staffed year-round [E8], making it a potentially lower-cost, lower-risk alternative that deserves real exploration before we install outdoor equipment. Get those answers first.

verdict.summary: Strong evidence of access gap (1.48 annual calls during closed-AED hours, ranked 2 of 100 schools) supports moving AED to 24/7 access. However, critical unknowns—exact call locations within ZIP, cabinet costs, vandalism risk, school permission, and FDNY Station 10 feasibility—preclude commitment without further investigation.
verdict.strongestFor: Area ranks 2 of 100 NYC schools for cardiac calls during all-AED-closed hours [E4]; current placement reaches 0 summer hours [E3]; bystander shock survival 66.5% vs 43.0% [E7].
verdict.strongestAgainst: Exact 2025 call locations within ZIP unknown [E9]; FDNY Station 10 staffed 24/7 only 136 m away [E8]; cabinet cost, vandalism risk, school permission all undetermined [E9].
verdict.nextStep: Map 2025 cardiac-arrest calls to precise locations; obtain FDNY Station 10 AED hosting feasibility and timeline; compare street-cabinet vs fire-station costs and vandalism risk.
